content: An Hfr cell, also known as an Hfr strain, is a type of bacterium in which a conjugative plasmid, often referred to as the F plasmid or fertility factor, has become integrated into the bacterial chromosome. The term Hfr stands for high frequency recombination, a characteristic first described by Luca Cavalli-Sforza. Unlike a typical F+ cell, which contains the F plasmid in its free, non-integrated form, an Hfr cell attempts to transfer its entire chromosomal DNA to an F− cell during bacterial conjugation. This process occurs through a structure called the pilus, which forms a mating bridge between the two cells. The integration of the F plasmid into the bacterial chromosome occurs at specific insertion points. Once integrated, the F factor retains its ability to initiate transfer to an F− cell. However, because the F factor is now part of the chromosome, the transfer process also includes adjacent chromosomal DNA. This phenomenon makes Hfr cells particularly valuable for studying genetic linkage and recombination, as well as for mapping bacterial chromosomes. The rate of DNA transfer through the pilus is consistent, allowing researchers to use techniques such as interrupted mating to determine the relative positions of genes on the chromosome. During conjugation, genetic material is transferred from the donor bacterium to the recipient through the sex pilus. The formation of the pilus and the ability to donate DNA require the presence of the F plasmid, which contains approximately 25 genes, most of which are involved in pilus production. Cells that possess the F plasmid are designated as F+, while those lacking it are referred to as F−. The F plasmid is classified as an episome, meaning it can exist either as an independent plasmid or as an integrated part of the bacterial chromosome. When the F plasmid integrates into the chromosome, the cell is classified as an Hfr cell. During the transfer of genetic material from an Hfr cell to an F− cell, the F plasmid may carry along portions of the chromosomal DNA. Importantly, the donor cell does not lose any genetic material during this process because the transferred DNA is simultaneously replicated. However, it is exceedingly rare for the entire chromosome of an Hfr cell to be transferred to the recipient. This is because the mating bridge, or pilus, is a fragile structure that often breaks before the transfer is complete. As a result, the F− cell typically receives only a portion of the donor's chromosomal DNA, which it can then incorporate into its own genome through homologous recombination. This recombination occurs when the newly acquired DNA aligns with homologous regions of the recipient's chromosome and undergoes genetic exchange. Although there is some debate on the exact mechanism of DNA transfer, it is generally believed that the pilus itself does not directly mediate the exchange of genetic material. Instead, specialized proteins are thought to create a channel between the two bacterial cells, through which the DNA is transferred.
